Roadmap

What comes next, in the order the milestone graph derives, each milestone gated by the ones it depends on being accepted rather than by anyone's intention.

A milestone here is an outcome, not a bucket of tickets. Its status comes from its own issues and from whether the milestones it depends on have been accepted — so finishing every issue inside a blocked milestone does not release it. That is why the sequence below is derived rather than written down. Each milestone's bar counts its accepted issues against the ones it requires; a full bar on a blocked milestone still does not release it.

Every milestone the plan holds is listed, in the graph's order, and none is left out for a field a person did or did not fill in. A milestone that has shipped shows the release that carried it and that release's date: the first release record containing its last accepted issue, inferred from the records and never typed. One no release has carried yet reads unreleased and shows the date of its last delivered issue, read from the history. Under it are its issues, grouped by their declared status, each linking to its own page. A milestone that names a claim shows the claim it would move out of planned. Naming it is not promoting it: a claim becomes guaranteed when an implementation, a behavioural test and a blocking CI job exist for it, and the guarantees matrix will keep saying planned until they do.

The order, and why it is not a preference

28 of 101 milestones depend on another, and the dependency is enforced rather than intended: a milestone whose dependencies are not accepted is BLOCKED whatever its own issues say. Its bar can be full and it still waits: the bar counts its own issues, the graph says whether it may begin.
